video.titulo: Mount Rainier: The Disaster Waiting to Happen
video.descricao:
Full clickable source links: https://tinyurl.com/sources-mountRainier

Mount Rainier ranks 3rd on the USGS national volcano threat list. Yellowstone ranks 21st. Here is what the hazard maps actually show — and why children south of Seattle rehearse walking away from it every spring.

Rainier does not need to erupt to kill people. The rock inside it has been chemically rotted into weak, water-saturated clay by its own hydrothermal system, and USGS confirms at least one past lahar — the Electron Mudflow, now tree-ring dated to late summer 1507 — came with no known eruption at all. They have a name for that scenario: a "no-notice" lahar. More than 90,000 people live where a large lahar can reach them, and Orting could be hit as little as 40 minutes after the warning sounds.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The Annual Uphill Walk
2:33 What Actually Makes the Mountain Dangerous
6:19 The Risk of a No-Notice Event
10:26 The Race Against the Clock
17:04 Practical Steps for Preparedness

Do you live within reach of a volcano — and has anyone ever actually shown you the route out? Tell me in the comments.

If this made the risk clearer, a like helps it reach the people standing in these valleys. Subscribe if you want the follow-ups.

RESOURCES
The Emergency Preparedness Guide — a large-print, plain-language plan covering earthquakes, volcanic hazards, floods, wildfires, extreme heat, winter storms, and long power outages, with fill-in worksheets for your family's contacts, documents, medications, and meeting points: https://payhip.com/b/GWENV

Sources include the U.S. Geological Survey (Fact Sheet 2008-3062, GIP 265, Open-File Report 2021-1118, SIR 2009-5211 and SIR 2018-5140), the Washington Geological Survey, Pierce County Emergency Management, the Pacific Northwest Seismic Network, and the 2026 Geology paper dating the Electron Mudflow. 

This video is educational commentary, not a prediction of an imminent eruption.

transcricao.txt: Every spring, thousands of
schoolchildren south of Seattle walk out
of class in the middle of the morning
and start climbing uphill away from
Mount Rainier.
Not away from a fire and not away from
any earthquake. This isn't a normal
school drill. They're walking uphill
away from a volcano that the United
States Geological Survey ranks as a
bigger threat to American lives and
property than Yellowstone. They follow a
marked route through town away from the
river and they keep going until they
reach the highest ground they can get to
on foot. It ran again just this April on
the 23rd. Puyallup, Sumner, Bonney Lake,
Orting, White River, Carbonado. Five
districts walking uphill on a Thursday
morning.
They go on foot for a specific reason.
Orting has already tested the
alternative and the drill showed that
putting students into vehicles does not
work. The roads clog up and the time
runs out.
Now, here's the part I want you to think
about before I go any further on this.
There is no eruption. There's no alert
happening, no warning in effect, nothing
on that mountain that a geologist would
call unrest. And yet every spring those
kids still walk. They're not rehearsing
for the thing that you might be
picturing. The ranking is worth being
precise about because people assume it's
all hype. In 2018, the USGS scored every
volcano in the United States, all 160 of
them, using 15 hazard factors and nine
exposure factors. Yellowstone, the one
that everybody names, placed 21st with a
threat score of 115. Mount Rainier
placed third with 203. Only Kīlauea, and
apologies if I'm pronouncing those
wrong, I'm doing my best, and Mount
Saint Helens scored above it.
Third in the country for Mount Rainier,
and most people outside Washington state
couldn't tell you the first thing about
why that is. Before I keep getting into
it, though, let me introduce myself
first. My name is Gwen and I'm an
amateur geologist. My husband and I
created this channel together just a
couple weeks ago and now we're hitting
over 10,000 subscribers and it's blowing
our minds. So, thank you so much. We
really love reading your stories. By the
way, if you want to know more, all the
sources and research for this video is
in the description below. I have a favor
to ask. Share in the comments whether
you live within reach of a volcano. And

actually told you where you're supposed
to go if it erupts. Not a vague idea of
where you should go, but an actual
route. I ask because the answer to that
question has everything to do with what
we're learning today. And if you want to
be updated on weather events, disaster
preparedness, everything else that's
happening on our planet, subscribe and
like to keep the channel going. Okay,
